column2: As long as there is any trace of poison in the body, how can there be health? So for the yogi, as long as the ego remains, how can there be liberation?
By the complete cessation of egoism, by the removal of the manifold imaginings it created, and by discrimination of the inner truth, one realises this truth: "This am I."

Give up at once the notion "I" in the ego, the doer — a modification that partakes of the Self's reflection and steals one's own state. By superimposing it on yourself, you, the inner Self, of the form of consciousness and of a body of happiness, have come to this worldly existence, full of the pains of birth, death and old age.

For you, ever of one form, the all-pervading Self of consciousness, an embodiment of bliss, of blameless fame, unchanging, there is no worldly existence anywhere except through the superimposition of egoism.

Therefore, having clearly cut off with the great sword of knowledge this egoism, your enemy, appearing like a thorn in the throat of the enjoyer, enjoy as you please the happiness of the empire of the Self.

Then, turning the mind's activity away from the ego and the rest, free of desire through gaining the highest goal, rest in silence, in the experience of the bliss of the Self, with the full Self, in Brahman, free of alternatives.
Even if the great ego is cut off at the root, if it is revived in the mind for a moment, it comes to life again and produces a hundred distractions, as a cloud does with the wind in the rainy season.
Having subdued the enemy, egoism, no opening should ever be given to it by brooding on objects; that is what revives it, as water revives a withered lemon tree.

One who stands as the body, a desirer, how can he be a desirer distinct (from the body)? Therefore the pursuit of objects, through leading to difference, is the cause of the bondage of worldly existence.
By the growth of the effect the seed is seen to grow, and by the destruction of the effect the seed perishes; therefore the effect should be checked.
By the growth of habit-impression, the effect grows, and by the growth of the effect, habit-impression grows; thus a person's worldly existence continues in every way and does not cease.
To cut the bond of worldly existence, the ascetic should burn both of these; the growth of habit-impressions arises from these two: thought and outer action.

Habit-impression is inwardly driven by these two; increasing through them, it produces the worldly existence of the Self. The means for the destruction of the three (thought, action, habit-impression) in all states, always,
everywhere and in everything, is looking on all as only Brahman; by the strengthening of the habit-impression of the truth, those three are dissolved.
With the destruction of action, thought is destroyed; thence the exhaustion of habit-impressions; the exhaustion of habit-impressions is liberation, and that is held to be liberation while living.
When the habit-impression of the true (Self) arises and expands, the habit-impression of ego and the rest dissolves, as the darkness, however dense, dissolves in the glow of dawn.
Darkness and its effects, the mass of evils, is not seen when the sun has risen; so in the experience of the taste of non-dual bliss there is no bondage and not a whiff of sorrow.
Dissolving the perceived world, contemplating only Being, a mass of bliss, and collected, either outwardly or inwardly, pass your time while the bond of karma persists.
Negligence must never be allowed in steadfastness in Brahman; "negligence is death," said the venerable son of Brahma (Sanatkumara).
For the man of knowledge there is no other disaster than negligence about his own nature: from it comes delusion, from that the notion of "I," from that bondage, from that pain.
Seeing even a wise man turned toward objects, forgetfulness distracts him through the faults of the mind, as a woman does her beloved paramour.
As moss, when pulled aside, does not stay away for even a moment, so Maya covers even the wise man who has turned away (from the Self).
If the mind, slipping from its goal, turns even slightly outward and falls here and there, it is like a playing ball dropped through carelessness onto a flight of steps.
The mind, entering objects, imagines their qualities; from careful imagining arises desire, and from desire, a person's activity.
Therefore there is no death greater than negligence for the discriminating knower of Brahman in absorption. The collected man attains success completely; be collected, be attentive.
From that comes the slipping from one's own nature; one who has slipped falls down; and for one who has fallen, except destruction, no rising again is seen.

Therefore one should give up intention, the cause of all misfortune, as a sick man discards unwholesome things. For one who, while living, attains isolation, that one is isolated when bodiless; the Yajur Veda declares fear for one who sees any difference at all.
Whenever this wise man sees even an atom's difference in the infinite Brahman, then at that very moment comes fear for him — because it is seen as different through negligence.

He who, in this visible world prohibited by hundreds of scriptural, traditional and reasoned arguments, makes his notion of Self, meets with suffering upon suffering, like a thief who does what is forbidden.

One who delights in pursuing the truth, being liberated, attains his own eternal greatness; but one who delights in pursuing the false perishes — this is seen in the cases of the non-thief and the thief.

The ascetic, giving up the pursuit of the unreal, the cause of bondage, should abide in the vision of the Self alone: "This am I." Steadfastness in Brahman, through one's own experience, gives happiness and removes the perceived pain that is the effect of ignorance.
Pursuit of the external increases only the fruit — bad habit-impressions, more and more. Knowing this, and giving up the external by discrimination, one should constantly pursue the Self.

When the external is restrained, the mind becomes clear; when the mind is clear, the Supreme Self is seen; when that is well seen, the bond of worldly existence is destroyed. Restraint of the external is the road to liberation.

What wise man, discriminating between real and unreal, taking scripture as authority and seeing the ultimate truth, would, knowing, take support in the unreal — like a child — a cause of his own fall?

For one attached to the body and the like there is no liberation; for the liberated there is no self-conceit about the body and the like. For a sleeper there is no waking, for one awake there is no dream, since their qualities have different supports.
He who, knowing his Self within and without, in the moving and unmoving, seeing it as the support, and abandoning all adjuncts, stands as the full Self of undivided form, is liberated.

Seeing the Self as all is the cause of freedom from bondage; there is nothing else higher than the state of being the Self of all. This state comes about when the perceived is not grasped, through steadfastness in the real Self.

How can non-grasping of the perceived arise for one who stands as the body, whose mind is intent on experiencing external objects and who performs the various actions? It must be striven for, in the Self, by the knowers of truth who have renounced all duties, works and objects, who are devoted to steadfastness in the eternal Self, and who desire ever-lasting bliss.
For the mendicant who has done the work of hearing, for the accomplishment of seeing the Self in all, scripture — "calm, self-controlled" — enjoins absorption in the Self of all.

The destruction of the ego, whose strength has risen, cannot be brought about suddenly even by the wise. For those who are not steady in the absorption called free of alternatives, there are habit-impressions of endless births in between.
Joining the person with the deluding notion "I" by the force of veiling, the projecting power distracts him by its qualities.

The conquest of the projecting power is hard to achieve without complete cessation of the veiling power. When the seer and the seen are clearly separated, like milk and water, the veil on the Self is destroyed of itself; without doubt he becomes free of obstruction, and there is then no projection if it were of an unreal object.
Right discrimination, produced by clear knowledge, having analysed the truth of the seer and the seen, cuts the bond of delusion made by Maya; the one so freed does not return to worldly existence.

For the liberated one, the fire of discrimination of the oneness of the higher and lower burns up the whole thicket of ignorance; what seed of worldly existence could remain for one who has attained the non-dual state?
The removal of the veil comes from right perception of the thing; the destruction of false knowledge and the cessation of the pain produced by projection follow.
This triad is seen from right knowledge of the rope's true nature; therefore the true nature of the Real must be known by the wise for release from bondage.
As iron in contact with fire, so the intellect, in connection with the Real, expands in the form of measure and the like; since this dual effect is seen to be false in delusion, dream and day-dream,
therefore the modifications of Nature — the ego and the rest, and all objects down to the body — are unreal, since they change from moment to moment; but the Self never changes.

The Self is eternal, non-dual, of one undivided form of consciousness, the witness of the intellect and the rest, distinct from being and non-being — the meaning indicated by the notion "I," the inner, a mass of ever-lasting bliss, the Supreme Self.

Thus the wise man, having divided real from unreal and ascertained the truth by the vision of his own knowledge, and having known his Self as undivided knowledge, is freed from them and attains peace by himself.
The complete dissolution of the knot of ignorance in the heart occurs when, through absorption free of alternatives, one sees the non-dual Self.

This imagining "you, I, this" arises through a fault of the intellect in the non-dual, undifferentiated Supreme Self; in absorption, all alternatives dissolve on the ascertainment of the truth of the thing.

The ascetic, calm, self-controlled, supremely withdrawn, patient, ever practising absorption, realises his state as the Self of all; thereby burning up completely the alternatives born of the darkness of ignorance, he lives happy, actionless and free of alternatives, in the form of Brahman.

Those who, collected, dissolve the external — ear and so on — and the mind and ego in the Self of consciousness, are alone freed from the bonds of worldly existence, and not others who merely talk about indirect knowledge.

By difference of adjuncts it (the Self) appears divided; on the removal of adjuncts it is by itself alone. Therefore, for the dissolution of the adjunct, the wise man should always abide in the absorption free of alternatives.
A man attached to the Real reaches the Real by single-minded devotion; the insect meditating on the bee becomes fit to be a bee.

The insect, giving up attachment to other actions and meditating on the bee, attains the state of a bee; so the yogi, meditating on the truth of the Supreme Self, attains it by steadfastness in that alone.
The truth of the Supreme Self is exceedingly subtle and cannot be understood by gross vision; it is to be known by noble ones of very pure mind through absorption with a very subtle mental activity.
As gold purified by heating in a crucible leaves its dross and regains its own quality, so the mind, giving up the impurities of sattva, rajas and tamas through meditation, attains the Truth.
When, by force of constant practice, the mind thus ripened dissolves in Brahman, then the absorption free of alternatives arises, which of itself gives the experience of the taste of non-dual bliss.

By this absorption follow the destruction of the knot of all habit-impressions and the destruction of all works; the manifestation of one's own nature, within and without, everywhere and always, comes without effort.
Know reflection to be a hundred times better than hearing, and meditation a lakh of times better than reflection; and the absorption free of alternatives is infinitely so.
By the absorption free of alternatives the truth of Brahman is clearly and firmly known, not otherwise, since the movement of the mind, being unsteady, is mixed with other notions.
Therefore, with controlled senses and a calm mind, practise absorption constantly in the inner Self; destroy the darkness made by beginningless ignorance by seeing oneness with the Real.
The first door to yoga is the restraint of speech, non-possession, freedom from hope, freedom from desire, and always a love of solitude.

Dwelling in solitude is the cause of the withdrawal of the senses; self-control is the means of restraining the mind; through calmness the habit-impression of ego dissolves; by that the yogi always has the steady experience of the bliss of Brahman. Therefore the sage must always strive for restraint of the mind.

Restrain speech in the mind, restrain that in the intellect, restrain the intellect in the witness of the intellect, and dissolve that too in the full Self, free of alternatives, and attain supreme peace.
With whatever adjuncts — body, breath, senses, mind, intellect and the rest — the mind's activity is joined, that state becomes that of the yogi.
By the cessation of those, the sage has right and complete withdrawal from everything, which is bliss; one sees the overflow of the experience of ever-lasting bliss.
Renunciation within and renunciation without are fit only for the dispassionate; the dispassionate person gives up attachment within and without, out of longing for liberation.
Attachment to external objects and, within, to the ego and the rest — only the dispassionate one steadfast in Brahman is able to give these up.

Know, O wise one, that dispassion and knowledge are the two wings of a person, like a bird's; without both, climbing the creeper to the top of the mansion of liberation is not possible with either alone.

For the one of extreme dispassion comes absorption; for the collected one, firm knowledge; for the one whose truth is awakened, release from bondage; for the liberated soul, the experience of everlasting happiness.

I see nothing greater than dispassion as a source of happiness for the one who has mastered himself; and if it is joined with knowledge of the very pure Self, it yields the empire of self-rule. This is the door to the young maiden of liberation, ever open; therefore, for your good, always fix your mind on the real Self, free of desire for everything.

Cut off hope in objects that are like poison — this is the very work of death; abandon pride in caste, family and stages of life, and avoid actions from afar; give up the sense of Self in the unreal body and the like; fix your understanding in the Self. You are the seer, mindless, non-dual, the supreme Brahman in truth.

Fixing the mind firmly on Brahman, the goal, setting the outer senses in their own seats, the body steady, disregarding the maintenance of the body, attaining oneness of Brahman and the Self, and becoming identified with it by unbroken activity of the mind, drink day and night in the Self the taste of the bliss of Brahman; what use are other empty things?
Giving up thought on the not-Self, which is impure and the cause of pain, meditate on the Self, whose form is bliss, the cause of liberation.

This self-luminous, witness of all, the knowledge-sheath, shines forever; making it the target within the knowledge-sheath, distinct from the unreal, experience it as the Self by unbroken activity of the mind.
Bringing it out by an unbroken activity free of other notions, let him know it clearly as his own nature.
Here, strengthening the sense of Self and giving up the "I" and the rest, let him remain indifferent to them, like a pot and the like seen clearly.
Setting the purified inner organ in one's own nature, the witness, mere awareness, and leading it gradually to steadiness, let him then behold himself alone as full.
Let him behold the Self freed from all adjuncts imagined by ignorance — body, breath, senses, mind, ego and the rest — as undivided in form, full, like the great space.
As space is one, free from hundreds of adjuncts like pot, jar, granary and needle, and does not become manifold, so the pure Supreme, free from ego and the rest, is only one.
From Brahma down to a blade of grass, the adjuncts are mere falsehood; therefore let him see his own full Self standing as the Self alone.

What is imagined through delusion is, on discrimination, only that (substratum) and not different from it. On the destruction of delusion, the rope is seen as what it truly is; so is the universe the nature of the Self.
You yourself are Brahma, you yourself are Vishnu, you yourself are Indra, you yourself are Shiva; you yourself are all this universe; there is nothing whatever other than yourself.
You are within, you are without; you are in front, you are behind; you are to the south, you are to the north; you are above, and you are below.
As waves, foam, eddies and bubbles are in their nature water, so all this from the body to the ego is only consciousness; all this is consciousness alone, of one taste, pure.

All this universe, known through speech and mind, is only the Real; there is nothing whatever other than the Real for one who stands at the farthest limit of Nature. Does anyone say that the pot, jar and the like are known as different from the clay? The deluded one says "you" and "I" through the wine of Maya.
Where there is nothing else — scripture, by repeated statements, teaches the absence of duality, to remove false superimposition.
Like space, stainless, free of alternatives, limitless, motionless, unchanging, empty within and without, non-different, non-dual — what is there to be known of the supreme Brahman itself?

What more is there to say here, in many ways? The individual is Brahman itself; this entire world is Brahman; scripture says "Brahman is non-dual." Those of awakened mind, "All is Brahman, I am Brahman," having clearly given up the outer, live having become Brahman, as ever-lasting consciousness and bliss — this is certain.

Destroy the hope raised by the sense of "I" in the body of impurity and, later, in the subtle body, which is like the wind; having thus known oneself as the everlasting embodiment of bliss whose glory is proclaimed by the Vedas, abide as Brahman.

As long as a man clings to this corpse-like form, so long he is impure and suffers from others, the abode of birth, death and disease; but when he sees the Self as pure, of the form of Shiva, unmoving, then he is freed from those; so scripture also says.
By the rejection of all the apparent things superimposed on the Self, it is itself the Supreme Brahman, full, non-dual, actionless.
